# Margaret Cavendish, Duchess of Newcastle-upon-Tyne
**Margaret Cavendish, Duchess of Newcastle-upon-Tyne** (née **Lucas**; 1623 – 16 December 1673) was an English natural philosopher, poet, fiction writer, and playwright. She was a prolific writer, publishing over a dozen original texts under her name at a time when women were largely excluded from publishing.
## Writings
She was unusual in her time for publishing extensively in natural philosophy and early modern science, producing over a dozen original works; with her revised works the total came to 21. She often would have her portrait engraved on the covers of her works so that people would know that she was solely responsible for the creation of whatever she wrote and then published in some way or another.
Cavendish's publications brought her fame and helped to disprove the contemporary belief that women were inherently inferior to men. Cavendish used them to advocate women's education: women were capable of learning and benefiting from education, and she insisted her own works would have been better still if, like her brothers, she had been able to attend school.

# Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy

Cavendish Margaret Lucas Cavendish, the Duchess of Newcastle, was a philosopher, poet, playwright and essayist. Her philosophical writings were concerned mostly with issues of metaphysics and natural philosophy, but also extended to social and political concerns. Like Hobbes and Descartes, she rejected what she took to be the occult explanations of the Scholastics. Against Descartes, however, she rejected dualism and incorporeal substance of any kind.
# Margaret Cavendish (1623–1673)
Despite her conservative political tendencies, Cavendish herself can be seen as a model for later women writers. She wrote dozens of books, at least five of which alone were on natural philosophy, under her own name, a feat which may make her the most published female author of the seventeenth century and one of the most prolific women philosophers in the early modern period. In addition to writing much on natural philosophy, she wrote on a dizzying array of other topics and, perhaps most impressively, in a wide range of genres.

We're used to thinking of gravity in the context of large masses – the whirl of planets, the inexorable pull of a black hole.
Relativity describes gravity as the curvature of a continuous fabric of spacetime, while quantum mechanics describes the behavior of matter and energy using the mathematics of probability. Both theories are marvelously successful in their respective realms, but their mathematical frameworks don't fit neatly together, leaving physicists without a complete description of how gravity behaves when quantum effects come into play. To find a door into this regime, physicists in recent years have turned to an experiment made famous by 18th-century English scientist Henry Cavendish, which could isolate the gravitational attraction between relatively small masses from Earth's overwhelming pull. The Cavendish experiment consisted of a torsion balance, with lead weights attached at each end of a horizontally suspended rod, and larger lead weights positioned nearby. The attraction between the nearby weights and those on the rod caused the rod to rotate, twisting the wire on which it was suspended, allowing Cavendish to measure the gravitational attraction based on how much the wire twisted. In 2021, a team of physicists described what was at the time the lightest demonstration of Cavendish yet – a measurement of the gravitational attraction between two tiny gold spheres, each weighing around 92 milligrams.
